lead: Water, waste and gas are the systems the whole crew uses, so they are the ones that go wrong. Check each at the pontoon with the technician, then give the crew a few firm rules for the week.

sections.title: Fill it yourself and make it last

qa.q: How do I make the fresh water on a charter yacht last a week?
qa.a: Do the sum on day one: 600 litres for 8 crew over 7 days is under 11 litres each a day. So fill at every marina, switch the heads to **sea water**, wash up in sea water and drink bottled.

blocks.p: The gauge reads only the tank the selector points at, so check **every tank**: at the panel and by looking into the filler. Deck caps for water, diesel and waste look alike: have each identified and marked before a hose goes anywhere.

list: Run the hose clear first, then fill tank by tank and stay with it.
Water spurting from a small fitting in the hull is the tank vent: that tank is full.
Never leave a hose in the filler overnight.

lines: 600 ÷ 8 ÷ 7 = under 11 L each a day
Not enough: fill at every marina

blocks.p: Do the sum on day one. A transom shower runs litres a minute, and heads set to flush with fresh water empty a tank quietly: switch them to sea water. Wash up in sea water, drink bottled water and keep the tank for washing and boiling. A watermaker runs only offshore in clean water, never in harbour.

sections.title: What the pressure pump is telling you

qa.q: Why does the water pump on my charter boat keep running with all the taps closed?
qa.a: A **leak**: a pressure pump that runs with every tap closed is losing water somewhere, so switch it off and let the base find it. If it runs on and the taps spit air, the tank is empty.

blocks.p: Sink and shower water is **grey water**: on most charter boats it goes straight over the side, so use little soap in a bay. Before you leave the base, see the cockpit drains and the anchor-locker drain run free: a cockpit that cannot empty itself is dangerous in a sea.

qa.q: What can I put down a marine toilet on a charter yacht?
qa.a: Only what has been eaten, and a little paper: that is the rule for the **heads**. Wipes block the pump, and the crew pays for the unblocking.

blocks.p: The rule for the **heads**: only what has been eaten, and a little paper. Wipes block the pump, and the crew pays for the unblocking. Try every toilet yourself at check-in, and have a weak flush written on the form.

blocks.p: How far offshore you may empty the tank is in the base's briefing. In some waters, Turkey among them, nothing goes over the side and each pump-out is recorded on a card. With a big crew a tank fills in about a day, so plan the emptying like a fuel stop.

blocks.p: Under way, pump the bowl dry and leave the lever on 'dry': a full bowl can siphon when the boat heels.

sections.title: Find every one and turn it yourself

qa.q: How do I tell whether a seacock on a boat is open or closed?
qa.a: A ball-valve **seacock** is open with the lever along the pipe and closed with it across, a quarter turn. One that will not move is never forced: it can snap off below the waterline, so the base frees it.

blocks.p: A **seacock** is a valve on a hole in the hull. A ball valve is open with the lever along the pipe and closed with it across: a quarter turn. Have each one shown to you and turn it yourself. One that will not move is never forced with a lever: it can snap off below the waterline. The base frees it.

blocks.p: Leaving the boat empty: heads seacocks closed, gas off at the bottle, pressure pump off. Before a hard beat close the heads and sink seacocks, or a low outlet floods back when she heels. A water-cooled fridge has its own seacock: open it again when you come back, or the fridge warms up.

qa.q: What do I do if I smell gas on a yacht?
qa.a: Close the **valve at the bottle**, then no flames and no switches, open the hatches to ventilate, and only then test the joints with soapy water. Bottled gas sinks: a leak runs down into the bilge and waits for a spark.

blocks.p: Bottled gas sinks. A leak runs down into the bilge and waits for a spark, so the gas locker must drain overboard and its drain must be clear. Every bottle, the spare too, stands upright in such a locker.

blocks.p: After cooking, close the valve at the bottle, let the flame burn the pipe empty, then close the knob. If no gas reaches the burner, look for the **solenoid** switch. Hold an oven knob in for 10–15 seconds after lighting, until the flame-failure sensor is hot. Lock the stove's gimbals in harbour and free them at sea. A bottle of another make is never adapted to fit: call the base.

sections.title: Dry at check-in, so any water is news

qa.q: My bilge pump keeps running: how do I find where the water comes from?
qa.a: Taste it. Salt water that keeps coming points to the seacocks, hoses, stern gland or rudder seal; fresh water only with the pressure pump on is a leak on the pressure side. A **dry bilge** at check-in makes any water news.

blocks.p: Take over a **dry bilge**: it is your baseline for the week. Lift the float until the electric pump runs, then find the handle and work the manual pump. On a catamaran ask to see every compartment of both hulls.
